hook: He escaped slavery and became its most powerful enemy, with his voice and his pen.

pages.x: Frederick Douglass was born enslaved in Maryland, around 1818. He never knew his birthday, saw his mother only a few times, at night, and never knew for sure who his father was.

At about eight he was sent to Baltimore, where his new mistress began teaching him the alphabet, until her husband stopped her: reading would make him "unfit to be a slave". Douglass saw it as the road to freedom, and paid white boys in the street with bread to teach him.

At 16 he was sent to a cruel "slave breaker" who whipped him every week. One day Douglass fought back, for two hours, and was never whipped again. "You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man."
In 1838, dressed as a sailor and carrying papers borrowed from a free Black seaman, he took a train and a ferry north. A day later he stepped off in New York, free.

In 1841 he spoke at an anti-slavery meeting about his life, and became the greatest speaker of the movement to end slavery. In 1845 he wrote his life story, naming his old masters. To avoid capture he went to Britain, where friends bought his freedom.

pages.t: What is your Fourth of July?
pages.x: In 1852 he asked a crowd: "What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? A day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim."
In the Civil War he recruited Black soldiers, two of his own sons among them, and went to the White House to press Lincoln for equal pay. He also fought all his life for women's right to vote.
He sat for about 160 photographs, more than any other American of his century, to show the world a proud, dignified Black man instead of the cruel cartoons of the time.
Douglass rose from slavery to become one of the greatest speakers and writers in American history, and fought all his life for equal rights.
pts: Escaped slavery and led the fight against it
Wrote one of the great American autobiographies
Fought for equal rights, including for women
